Yep — this one is my project configuration, not your Windows setup. Your log is very clear:

vite@8.2.2
requires esbuild ^0.27.0 || ^0.28.0

but the project has:
esbuild@0.25.9

So npm is correctly refusing to install an incompatible dependency tree.

Fix it

From your project directory:

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"

Run:

PowerShell
npm install -D esbuild@0.28.2

Then:

PowerShell
npm install

Then:

PowerShell
npm run dev

If npm still remembers the failed dependency tree

Do a clean install:

PowerShell
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force node_modules -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Remove-Item -Force package-lock.json -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
npm install

Then:

PowerShell
npm run dev

Don't use --force or --legacy-peer-deps

You might see suggestions like:

PowerShell
npm install --legacy-peer-deps

Don't do that here. The proper fix is simply to make the esbuild version compatible with Vite.

Your environment itself is now looking good:

Windows 10
Node 26.8.1
npm 11.19.0

The relevant dependency should be:

JSON
"vite": "8.2.2",
"esbuild": "0.28.2"

So this is a one-line dependency correction in the app I gave you.

If the next npm install gets past this but throws another dependency error, paste that one too — we can clean up the project's package.json systematically rather than using --legacy-peer-deps.

Ви сказали:

do i have to restart pc?

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Nope. You don't need to restart the PC. 🙂

After changing the Windows PATH, you just need to close the current PowerShell/Command Prompt and open a new one.

Then run:

PowerShell
node --version
npm --version
where.exe node
where.exe npm

If you changed PATH while PowerShell was already open, that existing PowerShell won't automatically see the new PATH.

If you want to update the current PowerShell session without closing it, you can run:

PowerShell
$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User") + ";" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine")

But honestly, closing and reopening PowerShell is easier.

Good news: npm itself is working now. 🎉

This error is simply because you're running npm install from the wrong directory.

It says:

C:\WINDOWS\system32\package.json

npm looks for package.json in your current directory, and you're currently in C:\Windows\System32.

Go to the project

Run:

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"

Then verify:

PowerShell
Get-ChildItem package.json

You should see the file.

Then:

PowerShell
npm install

Wait for that to finish.

Then:

PowerShell
npm run dev

In short

Your workflow is:

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"
npm install
npm run dev

Don't run npm from System32, and don't cd node either.

The node folder is just where your Node runtime is located; the project root is where package.json is.

If npm install gives you another error, paste it — we're past the Node/PATH problem now.

Yep — this one is my project configuration, not your Windows setup. Your log is very clear:

vite@8.2.2
requires esbuild ^0.27.0 || ^0.28.0

but the project has:
esbuild@0.25.9

So npm is correctly refusing to install an incompatible dependency tree.

Fix it

From your project directory:

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"

Run:

PowerShell
npm install -D esbuild@0.28.2

Then:

PowerShell
npm install

Then:

PowerShell
npm run dev

If npm still remembers the failed dependency tree

Do a clean install:

PowerShell
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force node_modules -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Remove-Item -Force package-lock.json -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
npm install

Then:

PowerShell
npm run dev

Don't use --force or --legacy-peer-deps

You might see suggestions like:

PowerShell
npm install --legacy-peer-deps

Don't do that here. The proper fix is simply to make the esbuild version compatible with Vite.

Your environment itself is now looking good:

Windows 10
Node 26.8.1
npm 11.19.0

The relevant dependency should be:

JSON
"vite": "8.2.2",
"esbuild": "0.28.2"

So this is a one-line dependency correction in the app I gave you.

If the next npm install gets past this but throws another dependency error, paste that one too — we can clean up the project's package.json systematically rather than using --legacy-peer-deps.


Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Ahh, yes — now that I know exactly which project you're building, your idea makes sense.

According to the reverse-engineering notes in the repo, the license is enforced by the GUI, not by AltA2DP.sys itself. The notes say the trial is 7 days, while the kernel driver has no license check. GitHub+1

So conceptually there are two separate things:

  1. Which driver Windows is using

    • Microsoft's BthA2dp.sys

    • or Luculent's AltA2DP.sys

  2. Whether the official AltA2DP GUI considers your license valid

    • trial

    • paid

    • expired/no license

The important part is that an expired trial does not inherently mean Windows automatically switches the driver back. The README specifically describes switching back as a separate PnP/driver-store operation: removing/uninstalling the AltA2DP driver causes Windows to fall back to its inbox BthA2dp.sys. GitHub

Your custom app could therefore be designed like this

                 Your app
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          │                   │
    Windows A2DP         Alternative A2DP
       mode                    mode
          │                   │
    Microsoft driver       AltA2DP.sys
                              │
                         Your settings
                         / codec config

And I'd actually make the UI explicit:

Driver

  • 🟢 Windows A2DP

  • 🔵 Alternative A2DP

rather than trying to make "license expired" silently change things.

For example:

Alternative A2DP
────────────────────────
Driver:       Active ✓
License:      Expired
Codec:        LDAC

[ Switch to Windows A2DP ]

Then if the user clicks it, your application performs the legitimate driver/PnP transition.

And yes, you can have Windows mode as the fallback

That is actually a pretty sensible design.

Your app could detect:

AltA2DP driver installed?
        │
       yes
        │
License/config usable?
   ┌────┴────┐
  yes       no
   │          │
 AltA2DP    Windows

But: I would not make your app inspect or manipulate the vendor's license to get around the expiration. You don't need to. Your app can simply treat the license state as unavailable and offer Windows A2DP as a fallback.

The repo itself documents that the driver switch is independent of the GUI licensing mechanism. GitHub

And honestly, given what we've built so far, I'd add this as the next feature: a "Switch to Windows driver" / "Switch to Alternative A2DP" control, with the current driver shown clearly. That would also make your app much more useful if AltA2DP isn't available for some reason.

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Exactly — and I checked the README itself to make sure we're not guessing.

The important distinction is:

  • License expiration ≠ automatic driver switch.

  • The README says licensing is enforced by the GUI, while AltA2DP.sys itself has no license checks. GitHub

  • The driver-switching mechanism is a separate operation. The alternative driver registers for the same A2DP hardware ID as Microsoft's driver, so one can replace the other. GitHub

  • The documented trial is 7 days, and the license is stored separately in the registry. GitHub

So your mental model can basically be:

                  Bluetooth A2DP
                       │
              ┌────────┴────────┐
              │                 │
       Windows BthA2dp     AltA2DP.sys
              │                 │
          Microsoft's       Alternative
            driver            driver
                                │
                         official GUI
                         license check

If the official GUI's trial expires, that doesn't mean the kernel driver suddenly decides "trial expired → uninstall me." The GUI/license mechanism and driver are separate.

Which makes your project more interesting 😄

I wouldn't make our app a replacement for the official GUI's licensing system. Instead, make it a proper control panel for the driver that's already installed.

And there is a lot we can add.

The README exposes a surprisingly large amount of configuration: SBC, AAC, LDAC, aptX, aptX HD, aptX LL, adaptive bitrate, buffer/transport parameters, current negotiated values, delay, errors, etc. GitHub

I'd build the app roughly like this:

🎧 1. Device dashboard

For every connected headset:

and it checks:

and when Windows is active:

This is probably my favorite addition.

For example:

WH-1000XM4
  └── LDAC 990 kbps

AirPods
  └── AAC 256 kbps

Gaming Headset

When a particular Bluetooth device connects, your app can apply its saved configuration.

The driver already stores configuration per Bluetooth address, so this fits the architecture nicely. GitHub

And I would not touch the license mechanism. The README explicitly describes the licensing as signed Ed25519 licenses with server-side trial tracking. GitHub

We don't need any of that for the useful part of our application. We can concentrate on making a really good configuration/monitoring UI around the driver's documented configuration interface.

Honestly, what you have working now is already the foundation for a pretty nice little "Alternative A2DP Control Center" rather than just a codec switcher.


Ви сказали:

oh also maybe you could like optimize our contraption, yeah it does look cool! ...even better than that one, but its laggy... and eats 5% cpu...

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

Ви сказали:

do i have to restart pc?

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Nope. You don't need to restart the PC. 🙂

After changing the Windows PATH, you just need to close the current PowerShell/Command Prompt and open a new one.

Then run:

PowerShell
node --version
npm --version
where.exe node
where.exe npm

If you changed PATH while PowerShell was already open, that existing PowerShell won't automatically see the new PATH.

If you want to update the current PowerShell session without closing it, you can run:

PowerShell
$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User") + ";" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine")

But honestly, closing and reopening PowerShell is easier.

Good news: npm itself is working now. 🎉

This error is simply because you're running npm install from the wrong directory.

It says:

C:\WINDOWS\system32\package.json

npm looks for package.json in your current directory, and you're currently in C:\Windows\System32.

Go to the project

Run:

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"

Then verify:

PowerShell
Get-ChildItem package.json

You should see the file.

Then:

PowerShell
npm install

Wait for that to finish.

Then:

PowerShell
npm run dev

In short

Your workflow is:

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"
npm install
npm run dev

Don't run npm from System32, and don't cd node either.

The node folder is just where your Node runtime is located; the project root is where package.json is.

If npm install gives you another error, paste it — we're past the Node/PATH problem now.

Fix it

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"

PowerShell
npm install -D esbuild@0.28.2

Then:

PowerShell

PowerShell
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force node_modules -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

npm install

Then:

PowerShell
npm run dev

Don't use --force or --legacy-peer-deps

PowerShell

Don't do that here. The proper fix is simply to make the esbuild version compatible with Vite.

According to the reverse-engineering notes in the repo, the license is enforced by the GUI, not by AltA2DP.sys itself. The notes say the trial is 7 days, while the kernel driver has no license check. GitHub+1

So conceptually there are two separate things:

  1. Which driver Windows is using

    • Microsoft's BthA2dp.sys

    • or Luculent's AltA2DP.sys

  2. Whether the official AltA2DP GUI considers your license valid

    • trial

    • paid

    • expired/no license

The important part is that an expired trial does not inherently mean Windows automatically switches the driver back. The README specifically describes switching back as a separate PnP/driver-store operation: removing/uninstalling the AltA2DP driver causes Windows to fall back to its inbox BthA2dp.sys. GitHub

Your custom app could therefore be designed like this

                 Your app
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          │                   │
    Windows A2DP         Alternative A2DP

          │                   │
    Microsoft driver       AltA2DP.sys
                              │

                         / codec config

The important distinction is:

  • License expiration ≠ automatic driver switch.

  • The README says licensing is enforced by the GUI, while AltA2DP.sys itself has no license checks. GitHub

  • The driver-switching mechanism is a separate operation. The alternative driver registers for the same A2DP hardware ID as Microsoft's driver, so one can replace the other. GitHub

  • The documented trial is 7 days, and the license is stored separately in the registry. GitHub

So your mental model can basically be:

                  Bluetooth A2DP

              │                 │

          Microsoft's       Alternative

                                │
                         official GUI
                         license check

If the official GUI's trial expires, that doesn't mean the kernel driver suddenly decides "trial expired → uninstall me." The GUI/license mechanism and driver are separate.

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

Ви сказали:

do i have to restart pc?

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Nope. You don't need to restart the PC. 🙂

After changing the Windows PATH, you just need to close the current PowerShell/Command Prompt and open a new one.

Then run:

PowerShell
node --version
npm --version
where.exe node
where.exe npm

If you changed PATH while PowerShell was already open, that existing PowerShell won't automatically see the new PATH.

If you want to update the current PowerShell session without closing it, you can run:

PowerShell
$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User") + ";" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine")

But honestly, closing and reopening PowerShell is easier.

Good news: npm itself is working now. 🎉

This error is simply because you're running npm install from the wrong directory.

It says:

C:\WINDOWS\system32\package.json

npm looks for package.json in your current directory, and you're currently in C:\Windows\System32.

Go to the project

Run:

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"

Then verify:

PowerShell
Get-ChildItem package.json

You should see the file.

Then:

PowerShell
npm install

Wait for that to finish.

Then:

PowerShell
npm run dev

In short

Your workflow is:

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"
npm install
npm run dev

Don't run npm from System32, and don't cd node either.

The node folder is just where your Node runtime is located; the project root is where package.json is.

If npm install gives you another error, paste it — we're past the Node/PATH problem now.

Ahh, yes — now that I know exactly which project you're building, your idea makes sense.

According to the reverse-engineering notes in the repo, the license is enforced by the GUI, not by AltA2DP.sys itself. The notes say the trial is 7 days, while the kernel driver has no license check. GitHub+1

So conceptually there are two separate things:

  1. Which driver Windows is using

    • Microsoft's BthA2dp.sys

    • or Luculent's AltA2DP.sys

  2. Whether the official AltA2DP GUI considers your license valid

    • trial

    • paid

    • expired/no license

The important part is that an expired trial does not inherently mean Windows automatically switches the driver back. The README specifically describes switching back as a separate PnP/driver-store operation: removing/uninstalling the AltA2DP driver causes Windows to fall back to its inbox BthA2dp.sys. GitHub

Your custom app could therefore be designed like this

                 Your app
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          │                   │
    Windows A2DP         Alternative A2DP
       mode                    mode
          │                   │
    Microsoft driver       AltA2DP.sys
                              │
                         Your settings
                         / codec config

And I'd actually make the UI explicit:

Driver

  • 🟢 Windows A2DP

  • 🔵 Alternative A2DP

rather than trying to make "license expired" silently change things.

For example:

────────────────────────
Driver:       Active ✓
License:      Expired
Codec:        LDAC

[ Switch to Windows A2DP ]

Then if the user clicks it, your application performs the legitimate driver/PnP transition.

And yes, you can have Windows mode as the fallback

That is actually a pretty sensible design.

Your app could detect:

AltA2DP driver installed?
        │
       yes
        │
License/config usable?
   ┌────┴────┐
  yes       no

 AltA2DP    Windows

But: I would not make your app inspect or manipulate the vendor's license to get around the expiration. You don't need to. Your app can simply treat the license state as unavailable and offer Windows A2DP as a fallback.

The repo itself documents that the driver switch is independent of the GUI licensing mechanism. GitHub

And honestly, given what we've built so far, I'd add this as the next feature: a "Switch to Windows driver" / "Switch to Alternative A2DP" control, with the current driver shown clearly. That would also make your app much more useful if AltA2DP isn't available for some reason.

The important distinction is:

  • License expiration ≠ automatic driver switch.

  • The README says licensing is enforced by the GUI, while AltA2DP.sys itself has no license checks. GitHub

  • The driver-switching mechanism is a separate operation. The alternative driver registers for the same A2DP hardware ID as Microsoft's driver, so one can replace the other. GitHub

  • The documented trial is 7 days, and the license is stored separately in the registry. GitHub

So your mental model can basically be:

                  Bluetooth A2DP

                                │
                         official GUI
                         license check

If the official GUI's trial expires, that doesn't mean the kernel driver suddenly decides "trial expired → uninstall me." The GUI/license mechanism and driver are separate.

Ви сказали:

oh also maybe you could like optimize our contraption, yeah it does look cool! ...even better than that one, but its laggy... and eats 5% cpu...

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

Ahh, yes — now that I know exactly which project you're building, your idea makes sense.

According to the reverse-engineering notes in the repo, the license is enforced by the GUI, not by AltA2DP.sys itself. The notes say the trial is 7 days, while the kernel driver has no license check. GitHub+1

So conceptually there are two separate things:

  1. Which driver Windows is using

    • Microsoft's BthA2dp.sys

    • or Luculent's AltA2DP.sys

  2. Whether the official AltA2DP GUI considers your license valid

    • trial

    • paid

    • expired/no license

The important part is that an expired trial does not inherently mean Windows automatically switches the driver back. The README specifically describes switching back as a separate PnP/driver-store operation: removing/uninstalling the AltA2DP driver causes Windows to fall back to its inbox BthA2dp.sys. GitHub

Your custom app could therefore be designed like this

                 Your app
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          │                   │
    Windows A2DP         Alternative A2DP
       mode                    mode
          │                   │
    Microsoft driver       AltA2DP.sys
                              │
                         Your settings
                         / codec config

And I'd actually make the UI explicit:

Driver

  • 🟢 Windows A2DP

  • 🔵 Alternative A2DP

rather than trying to make "license expired" silently change things.

For example:

────────────────────────
Driver:       Active ✓
License:      Expired
Codec:        LDAC

[ Switch to Windows A2DP ]

Then if the user clicks it, your application performs the legitimate driver/PnP transition.

And yes, you can have Windows mode as the fallback

That is actually a pretty sensible design.

        │
       yes

   ┌────┴────┐
  yes       no

 AltA2DP    Windows

But: I would not make your app inspect or manipulate the vendor's license to get around the expiration. You don't need to. Your app can simply treat the license state as unavailable and offer Windows A2DP as a fallback.

The repo itself documents that the driver switch is independent of the GUI licensing mechanism. GitHub

The important distinction is:

  • License expiration ≠ automatic driver switch.

  • The README says licensing is enforced by the GUI, while AltA2DP.sys itself has no license checks. GitHub

  • The driver-switching mechanism is a separate operation. The alternative driver registers for the same A2DP hardware ID as Microsoft's driver, so one can replace the other. GitHub

  • The documented trial is 7 days, and the license is stored separately in the registry. GitHub

So your mental model can basically be:

                  Bluetooth A2DP
                       │
              ┌────────┴────────┐
              │                 │
       Windows BthA2dp     AltA2DP.sys
              │                 │
          Microsoft's       Alternative
            driver            driver
                                │
                         official GUI
                         license check

If the official GUI's trial expires, that doesn't mean the kernel driver suddenly decides "trial expired → uninstall me." The GUI/license mechanism and driver are separate.

Ви сказали:

oh also maybe you could like optimize our contraption, yeah it does look cool! ...even better than that one, but its laggy... and eats 5% cpu...

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

Nope. You don't need to restart the PC. 🙂

After changing the Windows PATH, you just need to close the current PowerShell/Command Prompt and open a new one.

Then run:

PowerShell
node --version
npm --version
where.exe node
where.exe npm

If you changed PATH while PowerShell was already open, that existing PowerShell won't automatically see the new PATH.

If you want to update the current PowerShell session without closing it, you can run:

PowerShell
$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User") + ";" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine")

But honestly, closing and reopening PowerShell is easier.

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yep — this one is my project configuration, not your Windows setup. Your log is very clear:

vite@8.2.2
requires esbuild ^0.27.0 || ^0.28.0

but the project has:
esbuild@0.25.9

So npm is correctly refusing to install an incompatible dependency tree.

Fix it

From your project directory:

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"

Run:

PowerShell
npm install -D esbuild@0.28.2

Then:

PowerShell
npm install

Then:

PowerShell
npm run dev

If npm still remembers the failed dependency tree

Do a clean install:

PowerShell
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force node_modules -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Remove-Item -Force package-lock.json -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
npm install

Then:

PowerShell
npm run dev

Don't use --force or --legacy-peer-deps

You might see suggestions like:

PowerShell
npm install --legacy-peer-deps

Don't do that here. The proper fix is simply to make the esbuild version compatible with Vite.

Your environment itself is now looking good:

Windows 10
Node 26.8.1
npm 11.19.0

The relevant dependency should be:

JSON
"vite": "8.2.2",
"esbuild": "0.28.2"

So this is a one-line dependency correction in the app I gave you.

If the next npm install gets past this but throws another dependency error, paste that one too — we can clean up the project's package.json systematically rather than using --legacy-peer-deps.

According to the reverse-engineering notes in the repo, the license is enforced by the GUI, not by AltA2DP.sys itself. The notes say the trial is 7 days, while the kernel driver has no license check. GitHub+1

So conceptually there are two separate things:

  1. Which driver Windows is using

    • Microsoft's BthA2dp.sys

    • or Luculent's AltA2DP.sys

  2. Whether the official AltA2DP GUI considers your license valid

    • trial

    • paid

    • expired/no license

The important part is that an expired trial does not inherently mean Windows automatically switches the driver back. The README specifically describes switching back as a separate PnP/driver-store operation: removing/uninstalling the AltA2DP driver causes Windows to fall back to its inbox BthA2dp.sys. GitHub

Your custom app could therefore be designed like this

                 Your app
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          │                   │
    Windows A2DP         Alternative A2DP
       mode                    mode
          │                   │
    Microsoft driver       AltA2DP.sys
                              │
                         Your settings
                         / codec config

And I'd actually make the UI explicit:

Driver

  • 🟢 Windows A2DP

  • 🔵 Alternative A2DP

rather than trying to make "license expired" silently change things.

For example:

Alternative A2DP
────────────────────────
Driver:       Active ✓
License:      Expired
Codec:        LDAC

[ Switch to Windows A2DP ]

Then if the user clicks it, your application performs the legitimate driver/PnP transition.

And yes, you can have Windows mode as the fallback

That is actually a pretty sensible design.

Your app could detect:

AltA2DP driver installed?
        │
       yes
        │
License/config usable?
   ┌────┴────┐
  yes       no
   │          │
 AltA2DP    Windows

But: I would not make your app inspect or manipulate the vendor's license to get around the expiration. You don't need to. Your app can simply treat the license state as unavailable and offer Windows A2DP as a fallback.

The repo itself documents that the driver switch is independent of the GUI licensing mechanism. GitHub

And honestly, given what we've built so far, I'd add this as the next feature: a "Switch to Windows driver" / "Switch to Alternative A2DP" control, with the current driver shown clearly. That would also make your app much more useful if AltA2DP isn't available for some reason.

The important distinction is:

  • License expiration ≠ automatic driver switch.

  • The README says licensing is enforced by the GUI, while AltA2DP.sys itself has no license checks. GitHub

  • The driver-switching mechanism is a separate operation. The alternative driver registers for the same A2DP hardware ID as Microsoft's driver, so one can replace the other. GitHub

  • The documented trial is 7 days, and the license is stored separately in the registry. GitHub

So your mental model can basically be:

                  Bluetooth A2DP
                       │
              ┌────────┴────────┐
              │                 │
       Windows BthA2dp     AltA2DP.sys
              │                 │
          Microsoft's       Alternative
            driver            driver
                                │
                         official GUI
                         license check

If the official GUI's trial expires, that doesn't mean the kernel driver suddenly decides "trial expired → uninstall me." The GUI/license mechanism and driver are separate.

Ви сказали:

oh also maybe you could like optimize our contraption, yeah it does look cool! ...even better than that one, but its laggy... and eats 5% cpu...

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

Ви сказали:

do i have to restart pc?

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Nope. You don't need to restart the PC. 🙂

After changing the Windows PATH, you just need to close the current PowerShell/Command Prompt and open a new one.

Then run:

PowerShell
node --version
npm --version
where.exe node
where.exe npm

If you changed PATH while PowerShell was already open, that existing PowerShell won't automatically see the new PATH.

If you want to update the current PowerShell session without closing it, you can run:

PowerShell
$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User") + ";" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine")

But honestly, closing and reopening PowerShell is easier.

Yep — this one is my project configuration, not your Windows setup. Your log is very clear:

vite@8.2.2
requires esbuild ^0.27.0 || ^0.28.0

but the project has:
esbuild@0.25.9

So npm is correctly refusing to install an incompatible dependency tree.

Fix it

From your project directory:

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"

Run:

PowerShell
npm install -D esbuild@0.28.2

Then:

PowerShell
npm install

Then:

PowerShell
npm run dev

If npm still remembers the failed dependency tree

Do a clean install:

PowerShell
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force node_modules -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Remove-Item -Force package-lock.json -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
npm install

Then:

PowerShell
npm run dev

Don't use --force or --legacy-peer-deps

You might see suggestions like:

PowerShell
npm install --legacy-peer-deps

Don't do that here. The proper fix is simply to make the esbuild version compatible with Vite.

Your environment itself is now looking good:

Windows 10
Node 26.8.1
npm 11.19.0

The relevant dependency should be:

JSON
"vite": "8.2.2",
"esbuild": "0.28.2"

So this is a one-line dependency correction in the app I gave you.

If the next npm install gets past this but throws another dependency error, paste that one too — we can clean up the project's package.json systematically rather than using --legacy-peer-deps.

Ahh, yes — now that I know exactly which project you're building, your idea makes sense.

According to the reverse-engineering notes in the repo, the license is enforced by the GUI, not by AltA2DP.sys itself. The notes say the trial is 7 days, while the kernel driver has no license check. GitHub+1

So conceptually there are two separate things:

  1. Which driver Windows is using

    • Microsoft's BthA2dp.sys

    • or Luculent's AltA2DP.sys

  2. Whether the official AltA2DP GUI considers your license valid

    • trial

    • paid

    • expired/no license

The important part is that an expired trial does not inherently mean Windows automatically switches the driver back. The README specifically describes switching back as a separate PnP/driver-store operation: removing/uninstalling the AltA2DP driver causes Windows to fall back to its inbox BthA2dp.sys. GitHub

Your custom app could therefore be designed like this

                 Your app
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          │                   │
    Windows A2DP         Alternative A2DP
       mode                    mode
          │                   │
    Microsoft driver       AltA2DP.sys
                              │
                         Your settings
                         / codec config

And I'd actually make the UI explicit:

Driver

  • 🟢 Windows A2DP

  • 🔵 Alternative A2DP

rather than trying to make "license expired" silently change things.

For example:

Alternative A2DP
────────────────────────
Driver:       Active ✓
License:      Expired
Codec:        LDAC

[ Switch to Windows A2DP ]

Then if the user clicks it, your application performs the legitimate driver/PnP transition.

And yes, you can have Windows mode as the fallback

That is actually a pretty sensible design.

Your app could detect:

AltA2DP driver installed?
        │
       yes
        │
License/config usable?
   ┌────┴────┐
  yes       no
   │          │
 AltA2DP    Windows

But: I would not make your app inspect or manipulate the vendor's license to get around the expiration. You don't need to. Your app can simply treat the license state as unavailable and offer Windows A2DP as a fallback.

The repo itself documents that the driver switch is independent of the GUI licensing mechanism. GitHub

And honestly, given what we've built so far, I'd add this as the next feature: a "Switch to Windows driver" / "Switch to Alternative A2DP" control, with the current driver shown clearly. That would also make your app much more useful if AltA2DP isn't available for some reason.

Exactly — and I checked the README itself to make sure we're not guessing.

The important distinction is:

  • License expiration ≠ automatic driver switch.

  • The README says licensing is enforced by the GUI, while AltA2DP.sys itself has no license checks. GitHub

  • The driver-switching mechanism is a separate operation. The alternative driver registers for the same A2DP hardware ID as Microsoft's driver, so one can replace the other. GitHub

  • The documented trial is 7 days, and the license is stored separately in the registry. GitHub

So your mental model can basically be:

                  Bluetooth A2DP
                       │
              ┌────────┴────────┐
              │                 │
       Windows BthA2dp     AltA2DP.sys
              │                 │
          Microsoft's       Alternative
            driver            driver
                                │
                         official GUI
                         license check

If the official GUI's trial expires, that doesn't mean the kernel driver suddenly decides "trial expired → uninstall me." The GUI/license mechanism and driver are separate.

Which makes your project more interesting 😄

I wouldn't make our app a replacement for the official GUI's licensing system. Instead, make it a proper control panel for the driver that's already installed.

And there is a lot we can add.

The README exposes a surprisingly large amount of configuration: SBC, AAC, LDAC, aptX, aptX HD, aptX LL, adaptive bitrate, buffer/transport parameters, current negotiated values, delay, errors, etc. GitHub

That would be very useful.

🔄 6. Windows ↔ Alternative driver switch

This is the feature you were talking about.

Something like:

ACTIVE DRIVER

● Alternative A2DP
  LDAC / AAC / aptX available

[ Switch to Windows A2DP ]

and when Windows is active:

ACTIVE DRIVER

● Windows A2DP

[ Switch to Alternative A2DP ]

I'd make this explicit rather than tying it to license expiration.

📝 7. Profiles per headset

This is probably my favorite addition.

For example:

WH-1000XM4
  └── LDAC 990 kbps

AirPods
  └── AAC 256 kbps

Gaming Headset
  └── aptX LL

When a particular Bluetooth device connects, your app can apply its saved configuration.

The driver already stores configuration per Bluetooth address, so this fits the architecture nicely. GitHub

And I would not touch the license mechanism. The README explicitly describes the licensing as signed Ed25519 licenses with server-side trial tracking. GitHub

We don't need any of that for the useful part of our application. We can concentrate on making a really good configuration/monitoring UI around the driver's documented configuration interface.

Honestly, what you have working now is already the foundation for a pretty nice little "Alternative A2DP Control Center" rather than just a codec switcher.


Ви сказали:

oh also maybe you could like optimize our contraption, yeah it does look cool! ...even better than that one, but its laggy... and eats 5% cpu...

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

Ви сказали:

do i have to restart pc?

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Nope. You don't need to restart the PC. 🙂

After changing the Windows PATH, you just need to close the current PowerShell/Command Prompt and open a new one.

Then run:

PowerShell
node --version
npm --version
where.exe node
where.exe npm

If you changed PATH while PowerShell was already open, that existing PowerShell won't automatically see the new PATH.

If you want to update the current PowerShell session without closing it, you can run:

PowerShell
$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User") + ";" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine")

But honestly, closing and reopening PowerShell is easier.

Good news: npm itself is working now. 🎉

This error is simply because you're running npm install from the wrong directory.

It says:

npm looks for package.json in your current directory, and you're currently in C:\Windows\System32.

Go to the project

Run:

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"

Then verify:

PowerShell
Get-ChildItem package.json

You should see the file.

Then:

PowerShell

Wait for that to finish.

Then:

PowerShell
npm run dev

In short

Your workflow is:

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"
npm install
npm run dev

Don't run npm from System32, and don't cd node either.

The node folder is just where your Node runtime is located; the project root is where package.json is.

If npm install gives you another error, paste it — we're past the Node/PATH problem now.

Don't use --force or --legacy-peer-deps

According to the reverse-engineering notes in the repo, the license is enforced by the GUI, not by AltA2DP.sys itself. The notes say the trial is 7 days, while the kernel driver has no license check. GitHub+1

So conceptually there are two separate things:

  1. Which driver Windows is using

    • Microsoft's BthA2dp.sys

    • or Luculent's AltA2DP.sys

  2. Whether the official AltA2DP GUI considers your license valid

    • trial

    • paid

    • expired/no license

The important part is that an expired trial does not inherently mean Windows automatically switches the driver back. The README specifically describes switching back as a separate PnP/driver-store operation: removing/uninstalling the AltA2DP driver causes Windows to fall back to its inbox BthA2dp.sys. GitHub

Your custom app could therefore be designed like this

                 Your app
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          │                   │
    Windows A2DP         Alternative A2DP
       mode                    mode
          │                   │
    Microsoft driver       AltA2DP.sys
                              │
                         Your settings
                         / codec config

Driver

  • 🟢 Windows A2DP

  • 🔵 Alternative A2DP

rather than trying to make "license expired" silently change things.

For example:

Driver:       Active ✓
License:      Expired
Codec:        LDAC

[ Switch to Windows A2DP ]

Then if the user clicks it, your application performs the legitimate driver/PnP transition.

And yes, you can have Windows mode as the fallback

That is actually a pretty sensible design.

       yes

  yes       no

 AltA2DP    Windows

But: I would not make your app inspect or manipulate the vendor's license to get around the expiration. You don't need to. Your app can simply treat the license state as unavailable and offer Windows A2DP as a fallback.

The repo itself documents that the driver switch is independent of the GUI licensing mechanism. GitHub

The important distinction is:

  • The README says licensing is enforced by the GUI, while AltA2DP.sys itself has no license checks. GitHub

  • The driver-switching mechanism is a separate operation. The alternative driver registers for the same A2DP hardware ID as Microsoft's driver, so one can replace the other. GitHub

  • The documented trial is 7 days, and the license is stored separately in the registry. GitHub

So your mental model can basically be:

                  Bluetooth A2DP

If the official GUI's trial expires, that doesn't mean the kernel driver suddenly decides "trial expired → uninstall me." The GUI/license mechanism and driver are separate.

Ви сказали:

oh also maybe you could like optimize our contraption, yeah it does look cool! ...even better than that one, but its laggy... and eats 5% cpu...

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Nope. You don't need to restart the PC. 🙂

After changing the Windows PATH, you just need to close the current PowerShell/Command Prompt and open a new one.

Then run:

PowerShell
node --version
npm --version
where.exe node
where.exe npm

If you changed PATH while PowerShell was already open, that existing PowerShell won't automatically see the new PATH.

If you want to update the current PowerShell session without closing it, you can run:

PowerShell
$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User") + ";" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine")

But honestly, closing and reopening PowerShell is easier.

npm error code ENOENT npm error syscall open npm error path C:\WINDOWS\system32\package.json npm error errno -4058 npm error enoent Could not read package.json: Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open 'C:\WINDOWS\system32\package.json' npm error enoent This is related to npm not being able to find a file. npm error enoent npm error A complete log of this run can be found in: C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\npm-cache\_logs\2026-08-27T09_35_53_461Z-debug-0.log

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Good news: npm itself is working now. 🎉

This error is simply because you're running npm install from the wrong directory.

It says:

C:\WINDOWS\system32\package.json

npm looks for package.json in your current directory, and you're currently in C:\Windows\System32.

Go to the project

Run:

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"

Then verify:

PowerShell
Get-ChildItem package.json

You should see the file.

Then:

PowerShell
npm install

Wait for that to finish.

Then:

PowerShell
npm run dev

In short

Your workflow is:

PowerShell
cd "C:\Users\user\Downloads\alt-a2dp-control-0.1.0\alt-a2dp-control"
npm install
npm run dev

Don't run npm from System32, and don't cd node either.

The node folder is just where your Node runtime is located; the project root is where package.json is.

If npm install gives you another error, paste it — we're past the Node/PATH problem now.

Don't use --force or --legacy-peer-deps

npm 11.19.0

Ahh, yes — now that I know exactly which project you're building, your idea makes sense.

According to the reverse-engineering notes in the repo, the license is enforced by the GUI, not by AltA2DP.sys itself. The notes say the trial is 7 days, while the kernel driver has no license check. GitHub+1

So conceptually there are two separate things:

  1. Which driver Windows is using

    • Microsoft's BthA2dp.sys

    • or Luculent's AltA2DP.sys

  2. Whether the official AltA2DP GUI considers your license valid

    • trial

    • paid

    • expired/no license

The important part is that an expired trial does not inherently mean Windows automatically switches the driver back. The README specifically describes switching back as a separate PnP/driver-store operation: removing/uninstalling the AltA2DP driver causes Windows to fall back to its inbox BthA2dp.sys. GitHub

Your custom app could therefore be designed like this

                 Your app
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          │                   │
    Windows A2DP         Alternative A2DP
       mode                    mode
          │                   │
    Microsoft driver       AltA2DP.sys
                              │
                         Your settings
                         / codec config

And I'd actually make the UI explicit:

Driver

  • 🟢 Windows A2DP

  • 🔵 Alternative A2DP

rather than trying to make "license expired" silently change things.

For example:

────────────────────────
Driver:       Active ✓
License:      Expired
Codec:        LDAC

[ Switch to Windows A2DP ]

Then if the user clicks it, your application performs the legitimate driver/PnP transition.

And yes, you can have Windows mode as the fallback

That is actually a pretty sensible design.

Your app could detect:

AltA2DP driver installed?
        │
       yes
        │
License/config usable?
   ┌────┴────┐
  yes       no

 AltA2DP    Windows

But: I would not make your app inspect or manipulate the vendor's license to get around the expiration. You don't need to. Your app can simply treat the license state as unavailable and offer Windows A2DP as a fallback.

The repo itself documents that the driver switch is independent of the GUI licensing mechanism. GitHub

And honestly, given what we've built so far, I'd add this as the next feature: a "Switch to Windows driver" / "Switch to Alternative A2DP" control, with the current driver shown clearly. That would also make your app much more useful if AltA2DP isn't available for some reason.

The important distinction is:

  • License expiration ≠ automatic driver switch.

  • The README says licensing is enforced by the GUI, while AltA2DP.sys itself has no license checks. GitHub

  • The driver-switching mechanism is a separate operation. The alternative driver registers for the same A2DP hardware ID as Microsoft's driver, so one can replace the other. GitHub

  • The documented trial is 7 days, and the license is stored separately in the registry. GitHub

So your mental model can basically be:

                  Bluetooth A2DP
                       │
              ┌────────┴────────┐
              │                 │
       Windows BthA2dp     AltA2DP.sys
              │                 │
          Microsoft's       Alternative
            driver            driver
                                │
                         official GUI
                         license check

If the official GUI's trial expires, that doesn't mean the kernel driver suddenly decides "trial expired → uninstall me." The GUI/license mechanism and driver are separate.

Which makes your project more interesting 😄

I wouldn't make our app a replacement for the official GUI's licensing system. Instead, make it a proper control panel for the driver that's already installed.

Ви сказали:

oh also maybe you could like optimize our contraption, yeah it does look cool! ...even better than that one, but its laggy... and eats 5% cpu...

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

Nope. You don't need to restart the PC. 🙂

After changing the Windows PATH, you just need to close the current PowerShell/Command Prompt and open a new one.

Then run:

PowerShell
node --version
npm --version
where.exe node
where.exe npm

If you changed PATH while PowerShell was already open, that existing PowerShell won't automatically see the new PATH.

If you want to update the current PowerShell session without closing it, you can run:

PowerShell
$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User") + ";" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine")

But honestly, closing and reopening PowerShell is easier.

Ahh, yes — now that I know exactly which project you're building, your idea makes sense.

According to the reverse-engineering notes in the repo, the license is enforced by the GUI, not by AltA2DP.sys itself. The notes say the trial is 7 days, while the kernel driver has no license check. GitHub+1

So conceptually there are two separate things:

  1. Which driver Windows is using

    • Microsoft's BthA2dp.sys

    • or Luculent's AltA2DP.sys

  2. Whether the official AltA2DP GUI considers your license valid

    • trial

    • paid

    • expired/no license

The important part is that an expired trial does not inherently mean Windows automatically switches the driver back. The README specifically describes switching back as a separate PnP/driver-store operation: removing/uninstalling the AltA2DP driver causes Windows to fall back to its inbox BthA2dp.sys. GitHub

Your custom app could therefore be designed like this

                 Your app
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          │                   │
    Windows A2DP         Alternative A2DP
       mode                    mode
          │                   │
    Microsoft driver       AltA2DP.sys
                              │
                         Your settings
                         / codec config

rather than trying to make "license expired" silently change things.

Driver:       Active ✓
